How to Cut a Mandala on a Cricut: SVG Setup, Sizing and Weeding

By Super Mandala Lab · October 28, 2026

Mandalas are one of the most popular designs to cut on a Cricut, for vinyl decals, iron-on shirts, paper cuts and layered cards. They are also one of the easiest to get wrong. A mandala found online is often a drawing made of thin strokes, and a Cricut treats every stroke as a hairline outline. You end up with a design that cuts into confetti or won't cut at all. This guide shows how to make a mandala SVG that cuts cleanly the first time.

Why a mandala needs a cut-ready SVG

A Cricut cuts along paths. To get a visible line of vinyl, the machine has to cut around both edges of that line, so the line needs a real thickness. A plain line drawing doesn't have one.

The mandala maker's cut-ready SVG fixes this for you. It turns every line into a solid shape at the thickness you choose, merges everything that overlaps, and keeps only the outside edges. Design Space gets clean closed shapes, with no stray overlapping paths to cut twice.

Step 1: Make or pick a mandala

Start from a template or draw your own in the maker. For your first cut, choose a design with bold shapes and fewer rings, like the simple mandala or the heart mandala. Very fine designs look great on screen but are hard to weed at small sizes.

Step 2: Set the size and line thickness

Open Download, choose SVG, and set the style to Cut-ready shapes. Then enter two numbers:

  • Width. The finished size of the whole mandala, edge to edge, in inches or millimeters. Use the size you'll actually cut, because line thickness only makes sense at a real size.
  • Line thickness. How wide each line of material will be. Thicker lines weed more easily and stick better; thinner lines look more delicate.

As a rough starting point, try around 1.5 mm (about 0.06 inches) for adhesive vinyl and iron-on, and a little more for cardstock, which tears more easily at narrow points. Every material behaves differently, so cut a small test piece first.

The maker tells you how many separate pieces the design will cut into. One piece is ideal for a decal. If it says the design will come apart, make shapes overlap the ring next to them, or add a ring that runs through any loose band.

Step 3: Upload it to Design Space

  1. In Design Space, click Upload, then Upload Image, and choose the SVG you downloaded.
  2. Select it and add it to your canvas.
  3. Check the size in the edit bar at the top. The file is saved at the width you entered, but always confirm it, with the lock on so the mandala stays round.

If the upload shows up as several layers, select them all and click Attach so they stay in place on the mat.

Step 4: Cut and weed

  • Vinyl and iron-on. Weed from the outside in, and pull the excess slowly at a low angle. For iron-on, remember to mirror the design before cutting.
  • Cardstock. Use a fresh blade and a sticky mat. Lift the mat away from the paper rather than pulling the paper off the mat, so fine lines don't curl or tear.
  • Small details. If tiny dots or slivers lift up during weeding, the lines are too thin for that size. Raise the line thickness or cut the design larger.

Making a stencil instead

To paint a mandala on a wall, a sign or fabric, you want the opposite: the design cut out of a sheet. Choose Stencil in Download. The maker cuts the design from a solid disc and warns you how many areas would fall out, since any closed shape in a stencil cuts free. The mandala stencil template is built with wide bridges for exactly this.

Two-color layered mandalas

For a layered look, cut the mandala once in your top color. Then use Offset in Design Space to make a slightly larger outline of it and cut that in a second color as the backing layer. Stack the top layer on the backing.

Using a Silhouette instead

The same file works on other cutters. The free version of Silhouette Studio opens DXF files, and SVG import needs one of the paid editions, so if you're on the free version, download the cut-ready DXF instead. It has the same shapes at the same size.
